principles.text: Runs a leader scan every weekend ranking stocks by monthly performance, to catch leaders missed by daily scans and to gauge what is working; spends ~10 minutes going through the whole list.
Prefers to focus on software and biotech leaders because they move faster and are more liquid, easier to trade.
Wants to see more panic/selling (e.g. QQQ reaching its 50 EMA) before taking longs while many AI names are just starting downtrends.
Shorting bounces into declining EMAs (daily/weekly 9, declining 50) is how he maximizes reward-to-risk; three consecutive gap ups into declining EMAs favour the short.
Does not place shorts on a gap down into the daily 9 EMA (potential support); waits for a bounce into the unfilled gap / declining hourly 9 EMA.
Skipping the first hour after the open avoids dealing with the opening chop and lets him come to the desk with a fresh mind.
Intraday short trigger: waits for a 15-minute breakdown or rejection at the hourly EMAs/opening-range high, and checks QQQ for relative weakness.
For a long flushing into rising EMAs his plan is to wait for a close below the 9 EMA, using a recent swing low as a hard stop.
Parabolic/oversold longs are better when the indices are also extended to the downside; does not like buying a gap up into resistance.

Explosive acceleration in leaders (semis +100% in two months), declining breadth, strong oil and AI leaders breaking down ahead of the market make him bearish; acceleration signals eventual exhaustion and lowers odds of further breakouts.
Missing a bounce produced FOMO and poor trades.
A higher-win-rate short comes after one more consolidation or rejection (e.g. a pin bar) at the 21 or declining 9 EMA, shorting the next day.
Takes partial profits on shorts into swing lows/key support (e.g. a third off).
Prefers tech stocks because they are faster, more liquid and easier to trade, but traders doing well outside tech need not avoid it.

Shorts are more dangerous than longs because the market is in a bull market most of the time; avoids swinging shorts while the index is above the weekly 50 EMA - the best time to hold shorts longer is under the 50 EMA.
Uses no hotkeys and places stops separately from the entry order.
Prefers shorting near the weekly 9 EMA and does not like shorting when the market is already extended to the downside.
Prefers shorts as quicker swings; does not want a habit of swinging shorts while the market is above the weekly 50, since bounces can be powerful or V-shaped.
Defensive sectors tend to mean revert: when extended they pull back and base rather than run for multiple weeks/months.
Shorts: covers into weakness rather than waiting for a close above an EMA. Longs: trails with the 9 or 21 EMA, but about 50% of the time sells into strength; wants to improve long exits.
Sells more into strength because the last part of a run is often explosive and trailing with EMAs gives back a chunk of profits; willing to sacrifice upside to limit drawdown from the peak.
Tends to revenge trade or overtrade in drawdowns, so he avoids putting himself in post-run drawdowns that lead to deeper ones.
Scales risk per trade slower than account growth (e.g. +50% account -> ~+25% risk or less) to keep a buffer so he does not have to size down in a drawdown.
99% of the time ignores binary events like midterms; considers them irrelevant.
Cautious about adding shorts when the market is already too extended to the downside.
